video_title: Lori Calvasina, Managing Director, Head of US Equity Strategy, RBC Capital Markets
gist: RBC's Lori Calvasina lays out her valuation model (fair value ~8,150 on stressed rates and a 10% EPS haircut), a 'Tears of Fear' drawdown framework, the healthcare overweight replacing tech as an AI diversifier, Fed hiking-cycle history, and midterm sector effects. She argues the market is not in a bubble but that 2027 earnings estimates are the key vulnerability.

insights.claim: RBC's S&P 500 fair-value model regresses P/E on CPI, Fed policy and 10-year yields using data back to 1962 (excluding the 2010s, when those correlations were abnormal), then applies a roughly 10% haircut to bottom-up consensus EPS. With 10-year at 5%, three Fed hikes and ~2.75 inflation at mid-2027, it yields about 8,150 fair value, which is the official target.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Target is built on a deliberately stressed macro base case rather than consensus, so it embeds a bear-leaning haircut.
insights.quote: normally I look at, you know, a few other models and take the median or the average, but what I've been doing in recent updates is really just

insights.claim: Stress tests shift fair value materially: adding another hike with inflation at 3 and 10-year at 5.25% gives ~7,900; a scenario with 10-year at 5.5%, six hikes and 3.75 inflation produces a down market over 12 months. She says the market got close to, but did not cross, the 10-year yield tipping point.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Downside from rates is real but non-linear; no single yield level is the trigger.

insights.claim: The EPS haircut doubled from 5% to ~10% over the summer: first for fear the Iran war would hurt the non-AI economy, then for fear AI numbers are too frothy.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Street EPS risk is being priced in by strategists as a hedge on both the war and AI.

insights.claim: She expects another 5-10% drawdown, citing four risks: a longer Iran war, the midterms (volatile in 2018 and 2022), the rate environment, and 2027 earnings estimates needing to come down. Clients dismiss the first three as well-known but dig into the fourth.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Earnings-estimate risk is the least-hedged worry in client minds.

insights.claim: She discontinued her top-down S&P earnings model because the ability of macro variables to forecast margins broke down around 2015-16, as tech margins expanded relative to the rest of the index; she now relies on bottom-up company consensus.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Index-level margin forecasting is less reliable; concentration makes company-level work necessary.

insights.claim: Unlike 2022, the current equity PE headwind from rates is smaller because the 10-year move (~100bp+) is far less than 2021-22's 300bp+, resembling the late-2024 rise the market ignored, and earnings are a much stronger tailwind.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Size and speed of the yield shift, not the level alone, drive multiple damage.

insights.claim: Companies manage through shocks for a few quarters: in 2018 and 2022 current-year consensus held up, but next-year estimates (2019, 2023) were steadily drawn down from the prior summer. She applies this to Iran-war effects.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Expect cuts to forward-year estimates rather than the current year.

insights.claim: Hedges rolling off and inventories bought at lower prices being rebuilt at higher ones create room for downward EPS revisions. One food and beverage company said it could manage if oil stays below 100 but not if it stays above.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Margin squeeze from the war is deferred, arriving with a lag as hedges expire.

insights.claim: Capex bull case: top-10 market cap names (hyperscalers) appear to be leveling off at peak capex growth, while the rest of the market (Russell 2000, midcap) is in the early days of a capex recovery, tracking ISM new orders. The risk is that Fed hikes stall that catch-up.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Capex leadership could broaden beyond megacaps if the Fed does not over-tighten.

insights.claim: Major drawdowns correlate with outright contraction in NIPA corporate profit growth, not slowing growth; cutting trailing growth from +21% to +9% is very different from cutting to -5%.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Watch the sign of profit growth, not its rate of decline.

insights.claim: Non-US investors are more concerned about midterms, AI capex and rates, while US investors focus on earnings and bottom-up stock picking; the differing views on whether consensus earnings are too high are where the real debate sits.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: The US-vs-global sentiment gap is a source of potential positioning shifts.

insights.claim: She is not in the bubble camp: top-10 market-cap share of the S&P now matches their net-income share (no gap), whereas at the 2000 peak market cap exceeded net income share by about 10 points.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: No valuation premium over earnings share; either undervaluation or skepticism of earnings.

insights.claim: RBC took its tech overweight (upgraded mid-July) back off because the sector got expensive again and semiconductor earnings revisions began to decelerate, and replaced it with an overweight in healthcare.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Tactical rotation out of AI beta into a diversifier.

insights.claim: Healthcare thesis: valuations, flows, earnings and sales revisions look good, global analysts are bullish, and analysts rate it the best outlier if AI slows. Realized daily correlation of XLV vs XLK over six months is about -40%, making it an exceptional diversifier.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Healthcare acts as a hedge for the AI theme and tech.

insights.claim: AI is permeating every sector: utilities and industrials are expensive because they became pillars of the AI trade, financials discuss AI use cases, and the June energy conference was dominated by data-center power talk, making AI-independent diversifiers harder to find.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Sector diversification across AI is eroding.

insights.claim: Energy: RBC is neutral. Valuations and revisions look good and analysts are bullish, but flows haven't come and revisions track oil prices, which feels fickle. The Iran war has forced previously abstaining investors to look at energy again.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Energy is a headline-driven sector without 6-12 month conviction yet.

themes.theme: Drawdown tiers and Fed hiking cycles

insights.claim: 'Tears of Fear' framework: tier one is a garden-variety 5-10% pullback; breaking 10% typically goes to about 14% with few outcomes in between; tier two (14-20%, e.g. the 18.9% tariff drawdown) is recession near-misses; tier three is actual recession (median ~27%, average ~33%); tier four is ~50%.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Gives mile markers: hold your nose and buy near 10% if recession can be ruled out.

insights.claim: Her study of all drawdowns of 11% or more since 1956 found a median of 22% and an average of 26%; the 2022 drawdown of 25% fits tier three even without a recession. Another roughly 50% decline occurred in 1973-74 (about 48%).
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: A 25% decline in a bad non-recession is in line with history.

insights.claim: Fed hiking cycles differ: in 1994-95 and 2022-23 the average move was about 45-49bp and stocks dug a deeper hole; in milder cycles with ~25bp steps there was an initial ~10% hit and then stocks rose for the rest of the cycle. Current conditions look like the latter.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Pace of hikes matters more than count; don't map 2022 onto every cycle.

insights.claim: Attribution of the long-end selloff is mixed: oil, AI risk-off flows and other factors matter at different times and correlations break down. She personally fades the deficit explanation as a perennial criticism.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Equity strategists treat yield drivers as unstable inputs.

insights.claim: RBC analyst survey (+2 to -2): a Republican sweep scores a modest positive (below +0.5), a Democratic sweep a modest negative, and a split Congress about +0.09; sectors in focus are utilities, financials and energy, with healthcare the only positive under a split due to gridlock.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Midterm impact is mostly sector repositioning, not index-level.

insights.claim: Consumer staples scored negative in a Republican sweep (immigration, SNAP benefits), while consumer discretionary scored mildly positive in a Democratic sweep tied to lower gas prices after the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Lori Calvasina
insights.so_what: Sector-level political sensitivities are specific and policy-linked.
